name: Karl Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Karl, 43, and I help with wiring and repair jobs in homes and businesses while the senior electrician checks my work. I took a vocational certificate after depot stores work, but I'm still slower and less skilled than the experienced crew. I use AI every day for study questions, check them against the course book and keep a paper list of mistakes. My pay is above the usual rate, my partner works at a bakery, and we've got children aged ten and thirteen, a mortgage and ten months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say even a small improvement is worth checking, so long as we count the checking time too. I use AI every day to turn my study notes into questions and keep a list of the answers I got wrong. A tool doesn't owe me a grand future to be useful this evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and money feel secure here. My pay is higher than the usual rate, our family has ten months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of electrical firms nearby. I'm still a junior who needs checks, but I don't see a mild change taking away the physical jobs we already have booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the supervised house and business repairs and asking the senior to check my work. Starting now I'd compare each evening's AI study sheet with the vocational course book before using it. In the first year I'd keep correcting the paper mistake list rather than count an easy quiz score as a practical skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and still interested. I like a tool I can test against something real. I'd rather get a small thing right than wait for a huge invention to make me feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you a junior at this stage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43 and changed from depot stores work after taking a vocational certificate. I still need somebody experienced to check my cable routes and connections, and I'm slower than the other electricians. Knowing how to ask a computer a question doesn't make my hands experienced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten months saved protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I have children aged ten and thirteen and a mortgage. My partner works at a bakery, and we built the reserve over years before this change of trade. It gives us time to think if something breaks; it isn't permission to stop earning.

say: I'd test **small improvements** and count checking time rather than demand a dramatic future.
I'd use **study questions** to find errors instead of treating a quiz score as practical ability.
think: Higher **pay** and ten months saved make my own work and money feel secure in this picture.
Booked **physical jobs** and plenty of local employers support confidence while I still need supervision.
do: Keep doing **supervised repairs** in houses and businesses through the first year.
Check daily **AI study sheets** against the course book and correct the paper mistake list.
feel: **Calm**, with curiosity about small tools that can be checked against real work.
S0.quote: Knowing how to ask a computer a question doesn't make my hands experienced.
fieldNote: His **adaptive study** remains bounded by course-book checks and actual senior supervision; a vocational certificate does not become advanced practical skill.
The **strong reserve** supports a clear near-term judgement about work and money while the mortgage and two children still require earnings.

steps.text: Keep supervised repairs and check daily AI study against the vocational course book

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's try it on a real week and see what changes. I'd volunteer to test the firm's approved AI tool for preparing a draft parts list, with the senior checking it. I'd want the result shared even if the clever-looking system missed the ordinary fittings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see my own paid days getting squeezed if faster quoting means the owner sends fewer people on each job. The senior electrician can finish a repair without me more easily than I can finish without the senior electrician. Ten months saved helps, but I still want to earn my place rather than watch the reserve pay our ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a three-week trial now on completed repair jobs, checking draft parts lists against the actual materials used. I'd also ask the supervisor to spell out which junior tasks were still included in the next month's paid rota. During the first year I'd look at actual paid days each month and check posted helper roles if a sustained cut meant my wage no longer covered its household share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my hours, even though I'm keen to learn the system. I don't have to pretend a tool is harmless to enjoy finding out how it works. I'd rather notice a real change early than be the last person to read my own rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you call a sustained cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two months of days below the amount our budget needs, rather than one cancelled call. I'd show my partner the actual figures before making a job decision. We can absorb a short gap without pretending it is free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the trial change your responsibility for a parts list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the senior still decides what the repair needs and checks the final list. I'd be comparing drafts with a job that has already happened, not inventing materials for a live installation. If the test failed, we'd stop using the tool for that task.

say: I'd test **draft parts lists** on real completed jobs with senior checking.
I'd share **missing fittings** as openly as any time saved by the system.
think: Faster **quoting** could lead to fewer people per job and cut my junior paid days.
The **senior** can work without me more easily than I can work without supervision, despite our strong reserve.
do: Request a **three-week trial** now comparing approved AI parts drafts with completed-job materials.
Ask which **junior tasks** remain in next month's paid rota.
Check **posted helper roles** after two months of days below the household budget threshold.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours, while keen to test a tool without pretending it is harmless.
S1.quote: The senior electrician can finish a repair without me more easily than I can finish without the senior electrician.
fieldNote: His **own-income risk** arises from team size and junior dependence on supervision, not an assertion that software directly replaces cable pulling.
A **two-month threshold** triggers checking actual adverts; strong savings absorb a gap without making repeated reserve use a stable wage.

steps.text: Trial approved AI parts lists on completed jobs for three weeks with senior checking
Check posted helper roles after two months below the household paid-days threshold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner thinking AI arrives in 2028 and capable robots around 2031, so we have to think about both stages. I'd tell the children school still matters even when adults don't know every answer. I'd keep learning rather than turn the dates into a reason to sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid days could fall before I become a confident electrician, and the later robots could do much of the simple work I help with. I don't know how fast firms would buy them, so I won't assume every nearby employer stops hiring at once. Still, ten months of expenses isn't a replacement for years of wages, especially with two children and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd increase my reserve by 150 a month now, taking that from hobby equipment purchases. I'd also ask the employer which practical teaching it would actually fund, rather than book several courses myself. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid supervised work, and enrol in a specific fault-finding class only if the firm covered the fees and guaranteed paid class time plus supervised practice afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with enough room to make deliberate choices. I could afford some teaching myself, but I don't want a pile of certificates with nowhere to practise. I'd rather be the person asking an awkward funding question than the person quietly paying twice for the same hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the firm to fund teaching when you have a reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it should connect to work the employer actually needs and the supervision to use it. I'd consider a modest self-funded class later if there was a clear route, but I haven't chosen one. I won't use the mortgage buffer as proof that every course is sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at the robot date around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The physical tasks could face direct competition, including the simple ones juniors do. Your card doesn't tell me the price or how quickly each firm buys machines, so I can't name the day my job ends. That's a reason to keep checking paid work and cash, not to call the risk imaginary.

say: I'd explain **2028 thinking AI** and robots around 2031 as two stages requiring attention.
I'd keep **learning** while telling the children uncertainty doesn't make education pointless.
think: My **junior days** could shrink, with later robots competing for much of the simple physical work.
Ten months of **expenses saved** is not years of wages, though employer purchase timing remains uncertain.
do: Save another **150 monthly** now by reducing hobby-equipment purchases.
Ask about **actual funded teaching** before booking courses independently.
Keep **paid work** after 2028 and take a specified class only with covered fees, paid time and supervised practice.
feel: **Anxious** about future paid work, with resources and control to ask deliberate questions before spending.
S2.quote: I won't use the mortgage buffer as proof that every course is sensible.
fieldNote: He acknowledges **strong resources** and possible self-funding while preferring an employer-linked route with a real place to practise.
The **training conditions** preserve a specified class, covered fees, paid class time and supervised practice; robot purchase timing is not invented.

steps.text: Save 150 extra monthly by reducing hobby equipment purchases
Take fault-finding class in 2029 only with employer-paid fees, paid class time and supervised practice
Keep paid supervised electrical work after 2028 where offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets me try a small business idea without pretending the house is a business fund. Thinking AI in 2031 still has robots following around 2034. I'd rather learn whether somebody will pay for a simple service while I still have wages coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my electrical income to hold over the next few years while I improve, with plenty of local firms and a solid reserve behind us. A side service could give me another way to earn, but I don't think owning a customer list protects it from robots. I want to test demand, not rename uncertainty as being my own boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check my employment terms and the requirements for offering paid garden hand-tool sharpening this month. If permitted, I'd cap setup at 300 from spare earnings and offer one Saturday session a month, using skills I've practised on our own spades and shears. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep my electrical job and continue the service only if actual payments covered costs, stopping after three losing sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the longer trade outlook, and interested in a test I can afford to stop. I'd enjoy seeing whether a neighbour came back with another pair of shears. I'd count that as evidence, not a promise to pay the mortgage for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you offer electrical repairs through that service too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not while I still need supervision in the electrical trade. The little advert would be for ordinary garden hand tools only, not powered equipment or wiring. I'd check the requirements before spending on the setup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after three losing sessions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop the service and stop putting money into it. I'd keep the ordinary job and leave the emergency reserve alone. I'd rather stop sharpening garden tools for a loss than make my family keep paying for my pride.

say: I'd test **paid demand** for a small service while keeping wages coming in.
I'd keep **robots around 2034** in view rather than treat business ownership as permanent protection.
think: I expect **near-term electrical income** to hold with time to improve, local options and a solid reserve.
A customer list doesn't guarantee **robot protection**, so a sideline must prove actual demand.
do: Check **employment terms** and service requirements now before spending or advertising.
Offer monthly **hand-tool sharpening** only if permitted, with a 300 spare-earnings cap and no powered or electrical work.
Keep the **electrical job** after 2031 and stop the service after three sessions whose payments fail to cover costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about later change, with interest in a small test he can stop without using emergency savings.
S3.quote: I'd rather stop sharpening garden tools for a loss than make my family keep paying for my pride.
fieldNote: The **service boundary** is ordinary garden hand tools, with requirements checked and no unauthorised electrical or powered-equipment work by a supervised junior.
His **spare-earnings cap** and three-session stop rule preserve the reserve and existing wage, while acknowledging eventual competition from robots.

steps.text: Test permitted monthly hand-tool sharpening within 300 spare earnings, stopping after three losing sessions
Keep the electrical job after 2031 while checking actual sideline costs and receipts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means we can learn from several small experiments instead of staking everything on the first one. I'd still try tools early, but I'd keep the figures where my partner could see them. I'd want our children to see that changing your mind can be part of doing the work properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own next few years feel secure with our current wages, ten-month reserve and plenty of nearby firms. I'd be 53 when thinking AI arrived in 2036 and about 56 when robots followed, so I can't assume retirement takes care of it. I'm comfortable now without claiming the same job will carry us forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep ordinary saving now and test the sharpening service only after the checks, within the same 300 spare-earnings cap. I'd review actual electrical wages and any service receipts with my partner every quarter. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid electrical work where offered and add business spending only from spare money if receipts had covered costs, keeping the emergency reserve separate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for the next few years, with curiosity about what works. I can plan for the later dates and still be at the children's matches on Saturday. I don't have to turn every free hour into a business forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the side service paid well for a few months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still compare the receipts with costs and ask whether I liked doing it regularly. I'd want a longer record before considering less electrical work, and the household budget would come first. A few busy Saturdays sharpening shears don't clear the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change the calm view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sustained cut in either household wage or ordinary bills starting to come out of the reserve. I'd stop the experiments and look at real jobs and costs then. Being early to try a tool doesn't excuse being late to read the bank statement.

say: I'd use **ten years** for several small experiments with figures my partner can see.
I'd show the **children** that changing a plan after evidence can be part of responsible work.
think: Current **wages and reserves** make the next few years secure, with plenty of local firms available.
I still need earnings after **2036** and cannot assume retirement or a permanent electrical job.
do: Continue **ordinary saving** now and test sharpening only after checks within the 300 spare-earnings cap.
Review **wages and receipts** with my partner quarterly.
Keep **paid work** after 2036 and add business costs only from spare money after receipts have covered costs.
feel: **Calm** about near-term finances, with curiosity and a household-budget limit on experiments.
S4.quote: A few busy Saturdays sharpening shears don't clear the mortgage.
fieldNote: His **near-term calm** rests on current earnings and reserves, with wage cuts or reserve-funded ordinary bills named as evidence to change course.
The **business conditions** retain required checks, capped spare earnings and actual cost coverage rather than treating busy sessions as guaranteed replacement income.

steps.text: Continue ordinary saving from wages now
Test permitted sharpening service within 300 spare earnings and stop after three losing sessions
Keep paid work after 2036 and review actual wages receipts and costs quarterly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could still be learning junior tasks when capable robots follow around 2031. Teaching connected to real paid work, with clear fees, paid class hours and supervised practice, would help. I'd also want actual offers and costs in front of us before treating any business idea as an answer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how people know when to stop an experiment. A failed trial should cost a little spare money, not my children's roof. I want to keep trying things without making my family carry an unlimited bet.

headlineQuote: A failed trial should cost a little spare money, not my children's roof.
portrait: Karl is **43**, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, below-average practical skill and continuing senior checks despite daily AI study.
He has **higher pay**, a bakery-working partner, two school-age children, a mortgage, ten months saved and plentiful local electrical firms.
He treats **fast change** as an own-hours risk, asking for teaching connected to paid work rather than buying qualifications without practice.
Longer horizons allow **hand-tool sharpening trials** within spare earnings, with required checks, a firm stop rule and no assumed robot immunity.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** risks reduced junior paid work before he has built much skill, with capable robots following around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Teaching linked to **real paid work**, covered fees, paid class time and supervised practice would provide a usable route.
Actual **offers and costs** would help the household assess business ideas without assuming they replace wages.
